A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MpFL framework and PEARL-SGD algorithm. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting and relocation.

before.justification: V1 reports original simulations of quadratic minimax games, five-player quadratic games, and distributed mobile-robot control in Section 4.

after.justification: V2 retains original quadratic-game and robot-control results and adds an illustrative Local SGD comparison in Appendix B, Figure 4.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 retains the same per-player SGD updates, frozen opponents' strategies between synchronizations, and server concatenation/broadcast procedure. The constant and decreasing step-size rules are unchanged.

E1.justification: Both retain two-player quadratic-game evaluation through the heatmap, five-player quadratic games, and five-robot control. The new Appendix B comparison also uses a two-player quadratic game. Removing dedicated minimax convergence panels does not eliminate that problem class from evaluation.

E2.justification: V2 adds Local SGD as an evaluated comparator in Appendix B, Figure 4; v1's experiments compare PEARL-SGD synchronization intervals. This is explicitly an illustration of incompatible optimization formulations, rather than a standard MpFL benchmark. Other newly discussed algorithms are not experimentally compared.

E3.justification: Appendix B adds a diagnostic tracking player objectives over 100 communication rounds under joint-variable Local SGD versus per-player PEARL-SGD. The dedicated minimax theoretical/tuned-step convergence experiments are removed. Settings for retained five-player and robot experiments, including dimensions, synchronization intervals, tuning grid, and robot noise variance, remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 adds a failure-case study illustrating why optimizing the sum of player objectives can fail to reach equilibrium. The minimax-specific tuned-step analysis is removed, while the step-size/synchronization heatmap and five-player tuning analysis remain. Appendix E largely relocates existing analyses.

E5.justification: V1 explicitly describes five repetitions and standard-deviation shading for the stochastic minimax experiment. V2 makes five-run mean/standard-deviation reporting explicit for the retained five-player experiment and specifies five independent runs for stochastic experiments generally in its checklist. This clarifies reporting scope without establishing an increase in runs.

E6.justification: V1 Figure 2's four minimax convergence panels are removed. V2 Appendix B, Figure 4 adds objective trajectories showing an increasing objective under Local SGD and stabilization under PEARL-SGD. The retained heatmap, five-player curves, and robot-control curves are unchanged despite regrouping and relocation.

T1.justification: Section 2.2 extends the personalized-FL equilibrium formulation from a quadratic consensus penalty to a general convex coupling term, with player objectives hi + n phi. Appendix B adds an explicit quadratic counterexample illustrating the distinction from sum minimization. The main convergence assumptions, bounds, and proofs remain unchanged.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims: MpFL models clients as strategic players, PEARL-SGD uses local updates, and its convergence guarantees support communication savings in the stochastic setting. The scope of these main contributions is unchanged.

C2.justification: V2 qualifies which personalized-FL formulations are instances of MpFL and explicitly states the absence of deterministic communication savings under its current bound. Appendix E.2 adds an interpretation of robot-objective oscillations in terms of cooperative and competing interests; v1 mainly described objective reduction.

D1.justification: Appendix D newly discloses an Apple M3 MacBook with 16 GB RAM. The checklist promises source code and instructions in supplementary material, although actual availability is not established by the PDFs. V1's dedicated minimax data-generation subsection is omitted.

R1.justification: Appendix A substantially expands positioning through discussions of learning in games, strategic social behavior in FL, federated bilevel optimization, and concurrent Decoupled SGD. V2 explicitly acknowledges that Decoupled SGD has the same update rule and distinguishes assumptions and conceptual emphasis. New Appendix B develops the distinction from classical and minimax FL.

P1.justification: The document undergoes substantial restructuring: the main-text proof outline moves to Appendix C.1, the experimental narrative is condensed, and retained tuning and robot-objective discussions move to Appendix E. Related-work explanations are expanded, a dedicated comparison appendix is introduced, and a NeurIPS checklist is added.

P2.justification: V2 adopts the NeurIPS layout and places Algorithm 1 beside its explanation. It merges v1 Figures 4a–b and 5a into Figure 2, moves other retained panels into Appendix E, removes the minimax Figure 2, and adds the Local SGD comparison figure. These substantially reorganize the visual presentation.

improvement.justification: V2 improves conceptual precision by qualifying the personalized-FL relationship, acknowledging concurrent identical-update work, and illustrating the distinction from classical FL optimization. Hardware and repeated-run disclosures improve transparency. Removing the dedicated minimax convergence panels reduces supporting evidence, but the core theory and five-player/robot results remain intact, yielding a modest overall improvement.
